title: Spotcheck
pitch: A manufacturing quote request arrives as an email, a spec, and a drawing. An agent extracts the quote fields through WebMCP tools, each with its source. The estimator checks the flags and confirms.
about_excerpt: A manufacturing quote request arrives as an email, a spec, and a drawing. An agent extracts the quote fields through WebMCP tools, each with its source. The estimator checks the flags and confirms. Like Comment Story Updates Conflict on quantity: 750 in the email, 800 in the spec. Both candidates with their sources; the estimator picks. Missing values: where the agent looked and what it found instead. The seventh tool, a clarification draft, is registered. A locked field. The agent's later proposal comes back as FIELD_LOCKED and shows up as a suggestion the person can apply or dismiss. The clarification email drafted from the open gaps. The person edits and sends; the agent never sends anything. Confirmed: every edit, pick and open question kept, with the full change log naming both actors. Open your own package: paste the email and the spec, attach the drawing, and run the same prompt. The same session on a phone, replayed step by step through the same state machine. Spotcheck Your agent reads the RFQ. You spot-check it. A manufacturing estimator receives a request for quote as a package: a customer email, a purchase specification, a part drawing. Before anyone can price the job, someone has to turn that package into eleven fields: quantity, material, thickness, dimensions, tolerance, finish, delivery, drawing number, revision. Reading three documents for eleven values is slow. The real cost is the one value that was wrong and looked fine. An extraction error nobody catches becomes a wrong price in the quote, and the shop finds out after the purchase order. Spotcheck is a review workspace where the agent does the reading and the person does the checking. The agent works through the package with tools the page exposes over WebMCP, proposes a value for each field with the exact place it came from, and flags where the sources disagree or say nothing. The estimator checks each flag against the highlighted source, fixes what is wrong, and confirms. Live: https://spotcheck-rfq.vercel.app Why this use case fits WebMCP The estimator's browser already holds the documents, the review state, and the person who signs off on the quote. Sending the package to an outside extraction service would mean uploading a customer's documents and trusting a result that arrives without its evidence. With WebMCP the agent works inside the page, on the estimator's machine. Every value it proposes carries the id of the region it read, so the page can highlight the source and the person can check it in one click. The page also decides what the agent may do. That is the second reason WebMCP fits. Spotcheck's tool contract is asymmetric on purpose. The agent gets tools to list the package, read it one section at a time, propose a field value with its sources, report a conflict between sources, report a value as missing after a search, and draft a clarification email once gaps exist. Verifying, editing, picking between candidates, marking a field not required, sending the email and confirming the quote request have no tool at all. They exist only as UI actions. The reducer that owns the state has two dispatchers, one for the agent and one for the person, and the tool module imports only the agent's. The boundary is a property of the code, checked by the type system and by tests. No prompt can talk the agent across it. How it makes the estimator's work better The field list is ordered by risk: conflicts first, then missing values, then proposals waiting for a look, then everything else. Each row shows the value, its state, and provenance links that scroll the source pane to the cited paragraph or drawing callout and highlight it. Clicking a highlighted region focuses its field, so the link works in both directions. A conflict row shows both candidates side by side, each with its sources and the agent's note, and a Pick button. A missing row shows where the agent looked and what it found instead. In the sample package the specification's tolerance line is a bracketed template placeholder, and the agent reports it as missing instead of proposing the placeholder as a value. When gaps exist, a seventh tool appears in the browser's site-tools panel and the agent can draft a clarification email. The person edits and sends it, and the page marks the fields it covers as awaiting the customer. Once a person has touched a field, the page locks it. A later proposal on that field gets a structured FIELD_LOCKED answer with the current value, and the person sees a suggestion card to apply or dismiss. The agent never overwrites a human decision. The person reads a few flags, not three documents. Confirm stays disabled until every field is settled, and a line names what still blocks it. The confirm summary keeps every decision: each edit as "agent X → yours Y", each pick with the losing candidate, and the full change log with both actors named. What people and agents can do together now Spot-check instead of re-read. The estimator reads the places the agent flagged, not the whole package. In the recorded sample session (GPT-5.6 in the ChatGPT desktop browser; press Play sample session to watch it) the agent read the package and, within 34 calls, proposed nine fields, reported two conflicts (quantity 750 vs 800; "Rev A" in the email vs no revision on the sheet) and two missing values. The first proposals landed 44 seconds after the first read. Disagree safely. When the person and the agent disagree, the person's value stands and the agent's stays visible with its evidence. Asked to re-check an edited field, the agent reads the spec again, reports what the sources say, and leaves the entry as it is. Ask the customer with the agent's draft. Gaps become a clarification email drafted from the open questions. The person edits and sends; the change log keeps the difference between the draft and what went out. See exactly what the agent read. Reads are one section per call and every read is logged, so the person knows what left the page and when. Carry the result on without a hand-off button. After confirm, the read tools keep answering and the write tools return SESSION_CONFIRMED . "What did we decide on material?" and "give me the confirmed fields as a table" both work, and the agent takes the values wherever the quote gets priced. The page holds the state; the agent moves it. Two job stories behind the design (from a discovery pass, not from interviews): when a quote request lands, I want to know which values conflict before I start pricing, so that I do not quote 800 pieces the customer meant to be 750. When I have already corrected a value, I want the agent's later opinion to stay visible without changing mine, so that I keep control and still catch my own mistakes. How WebMCP is implemented One module, src/webmcp-tools.ts , registers seven tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : list_rfq_documents , read_document , propose_field , report_conflict , report_missing , get_review_state , and draft_clarificati
video_transcript_excerpt: This is spot check. A customer's RFQ package, an email, a spec, a drawing. The agent has just read it through the web MCP tools this page exposes. For each field it proposed a value and the exact place it came from. It starts on an empty page. The strip says what to ask your agent. One prompt in chat GPT and the page goes live. The agent lists the documents and reads every section, one call each. The drawing is part of the package. Regions on the sheet count as sources and the sheet zooms. Where the email and the spec disagree, the agent doesn't choose. It reports a conflict with both candidates and their sources. The estimator picks. Where the package has no answer, it reports the gap and where it looked. The moment a gap exists, the page registers one more tool, a clarification draft. Watch the count in the strip, six to seven. The estimator can change anything. Here the material goes to a different alloy. Ask for the clarification email and the agent drafts it inside the page covering just the open gaps. The person edits and sends. The agent never sends anything. Now ask it to recheck the edited material. It reads the spec again and answers. The sources say 6061 T6 and your entry stays as it is. A human decision is final. Once a person has touched a field, every right tool gets field locked back. The rest is the estimator's work. Pick a candidate, mark what the customer will confirm at PO, add the unit the drawing never stated. Verify what's left and confirm. The summary keeps every decision, what was picked, what was edited, what is still with the customer. Same tools, your documents. Paste an email and a spec, attach a drawing, run the same prompt. This sheet has no title block, so the agent reports the drawing number as missing instead of guessing. The agent proposes. Only a person can mark a field verified, change it or confirm. That split is the whole design.

live_observation.first_impression: Spotcheck opens a sample RFQ review with Email/Spec/Drawing tabs and a disabled confirmation button because fields are not extracted.
live_observation.after_state: The session became Live, reported 6 tools and 2 calls, and populated a review with Enter value/Mark not required controls while confirmation remained disabled.
live_observation.notes: The sample demonstrates agent extraction plus estimator review and change-log visibility.
